items.readable_text:
Content:
To take the transpose of a matrix, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row [MATH: 1] becomes column [MATH: 1,] row [MATH: 2] becomes column [MATH: 2,] and so on. A superscript [MATH: {}^{T}] is used to denote the transpose operation.

Content:
For example, the transpose of the [MATH: 2 \times 3] matrix [MATH: {X}] is the following [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix [MATH: X^T\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {X} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4} \
{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad\implies\qquad

{X}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3} \
{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1} \
{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
}
\right\rbrack]

Content:
The first row of [MATH: X] becomes the first column of [MATH: X^T,] and the second row of [MATH: X] becomes the second column of [MATH: X^T.]

Content:
Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

Content:
> When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from [MATH: m \times n] to [MATH: n \times m.]

Content:
Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
5 \
4 \
2
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad \implies\qquad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
5 & 4 & 2
}
\right\rbrack]

Content:
Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

Content:
[MATH: {B} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
8 & -10 & 0 & 6
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad\implies\qquad

{B}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
8 \
-10 \
0 \
6
}
\right\rbrack]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if [MATH: B=A^T,] then [MATH: b_{ij}=a_{ji}] for all values of [MATH: i] and [MATH: j.]

Content:
Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with [MATH: i=j]) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal. For example,

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad \implies\qquad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & 1 \
\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack.]

Content:
Also, transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix [MATH: A,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \left( A^T\right)^T = A.]

Content:
This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of [MATH: A] for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\quad \implies\quad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & 1 \
\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\quad \implies\quad

\left( {A}^T\right)^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack =A.]

Content:
Finally, for any numbers [MATH: c_1,c_2] and any [MATH: m \times n] matrices [MATH: A,B] we have the following rule:

Content:
[MATH: (c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To take the transpose of a matrix, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row [MATH: 1] becomes column [MATH: 1,] row [MATH: 2] becomes column [MATH: 2,] and so on. A superscript [MATH: {}^{T}] is used to denote the transpose operation.

Content:
For example, the transpose of the [MATH: 2 \times 3] matrix [MATH: {X}] is the following [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix [MATH: X^T\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {X} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4} \
{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad\implies\qquad

{X}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3} \
{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1} \
{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
}
\right\rbrack]

Content:
The first row of [MATH: X] becomes the first column of [MATH: X^T,] and the second row of [MATH: X] becomes the second column of [MATH: X^T.]

Content:
Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

Content:
> When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from [MATH: m \times n] to [MATH: n \times m.]

Content:
Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
5 \
4 \
2
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad \implies\qquad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
5 & 4 & 2
}
\right\rbrack]

Content:
Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

Content:
[MATH: {B} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
8 & -10 & 0 & 6
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad\implies\qquad

{B}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
8 \
-10 \
0 \
6
}
\right\rbrack]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Properties of the Transpose of a Matrix

Content:
Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if [MATH: B=A^T,] then [MATH: b_{ij}=a_{ji}] for all values of [MATH: i] and [MATH: j.]

Content:
Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with [MATH: i=j]) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal. For example,

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\qquad \implies\qquad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & 1 \
\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack.]

Content:
Also, transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix [MATH: A,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \left( A^T\right)^T = A.]

Content:
This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of [MATH: A] for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

Content:
[MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\quad \implies\quad

{A}^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & 1 \
\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack

\quad \implies\quad

\left( {A}^T\right)^T =
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7} \
1 & \color{red}{6}
}
\right\rbrack =A.]

Content:
Finally, for any numbers [MATH: c_1,c_2] and any [MATH: m \times n] matrices [MATH: A,B] we have the following rule:

Content:
[MATH: (c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T]
